kurz: How the three layers of retirement provision are taxed, how tightly they tie up the money and which layer suits which money.

bloecke.md:
The three-layer model (Drei-Schichten-Modell) is a tax-law classification of retirement provision. It does not promote particular products and does not set an order of priority. It came about after the Federal Constitutional Court (BVerfG) declared in 2002 (2 BvL 17/99) that the different taxation of civil servants' pensions and statutory pensions was unconstitutional. The legislature had to make amendments by 2005. The Retirement Income Act (Alterseinkünftegesetz) then arranged retirement provision according to its tax treatment. The first and second layers are only taxed on payout and differ in their state support and in the conditions of payout. The third layer is built up from income that has already been taxed. Providers and asset classes play no role in the classification.

The more the state subsidises contributions, the more tightly it ties up the money. In German retirement provision, state support and availability are therefore inversely related. This rule makes it easy to tell the three layers apart. Savers who look only at the tax advantage enter into a commitment that cannot be undone later.

bloecke.titel: State support and availability in the three layers
bloecke.unter: From the lowest to the highest layer, state support decreases and freedom of disposal increases; the model is built around this contrast.

stufen.text: Securities account, unit-linked insurance policy, property. No state support and no age limit, available at any time and inheritable.
Riester or, from 2027, the retirement investment account, occupational pension. Allowances or exemption from tax and contributions today, full tax liability later.
Statutory pension, professional pension scheme, Rürup. High special expense deduction, but only a lifelong pension, no access, hardly inheritable.

bloecke.md:
## Basic retirement provision (layer 1)

Basic retirement provision (Basisversorgung) comprises the statutory pension insurance, the professional pension schemes (Versorgungswerke), the old-age security scheme for farmers (Alterssicherung der Landwirte) and the private basic pension (Basisrente) or Rürup pension (Rürup-Rente). What they have in common is the legal structure of the entitlement; the return plays no role in the classification. Only a lifelong life annuity is paid out, for contracts from 2012 at the earliest from age 62. The entitlement cannot be terminated, capitalised, pledged or transferred. It can only be inherited in part, namely through separately paid add-on components such as an annuity guarantee period (Rentengarantiezeit) or survivors' cover. In return, the capital is protected against seizure and insolvency (Section 851c ZPO, Code of Civil Procedure). For the self-employed, this protection is often the most important reason to use this layer.

For tax purposes, contributions have been 100% deductible as special expenses (Sonderausgaben) since 2023 (Section 10(1) no. 2 and (3) EStG, Income Tax Act). The maximum amount is linked to the maximum contribution to the miners' pension insurance (knappschaftliche Rentenversicherung). In 2026, it is €30,826 for single people and €61,652 with joint assessment. Contributions to the statutory pension, with both the employee and the employer share, count in full towards this maximum.

An employee with a gross annual salary of €60,000 pays 18.6% into the statutory pension together with her employer in 2026, that is €11,160. Of the maximum amount of €30,826, this leaves €19,666 that she could additionally pay into a basic pension and deduct. As a single person, after lump-sum allowances and social security contributions she has a taxable income of around €47,000 and a marginal tax rate of around 34%. Because this rate falls as the deduction grows, the full deduction would reduce her income tax by around €6,000 a year. The precondition is that she has the €19,666 to spare and accepts that she cannot get at this money until her pension starts.

## Deferred taxation

With deferred taxation (nachgelagerte Besteuerung), the tax is shifted from the contribution to the payout, so it amounts to a deferral. For pensions starting in 2026, 84% of the statutory pension and the basic pension is taxable for life (Section 22 no. 1 sentence 3 letter a double letter aa EStG). This share depends on the year the pension starts and does not change after that. This rule is called the [[Cohort principle (Kohortenprinzip)|cohort principle (Kohortenprinzip)]]. Since the Growth Opportunities Act (Wachstumschancengesetz), the share has only been rising by 0.5 percentage points per cohort. Full taxation therefore only applies to pensions starting from 2058 instead of from 2040 as previously planned.

What is often overlooked is that the tax-free 16% is fixed once as a euro amount in the first full year of the pension and is not increased after that. Every later pension adjustment is therefore 100% taxable. On 1 July 2026, the adjustment was 4.24%, raising the current pension value (aktueller Rentenwert) to €42.52 per earnings point (Entgeltpunkt). The taxable part of a pension in payment thus grows over the years, even though the cohort's taxable share formally stays the same.

bloecke.titel: Taxable share by year of pension start
bloecke.unter: The percentage in the year the pension starts applies for life; later cohorts permanently pay tax on a higher share.

bloecke.md:
## Subsidised supplementary provision (layer 2)

The second layer is funded and tied to a subsidised purpose. Its payouts are fully taxable (Section 22 no. 5 EStG). It has two branches.

The private branch is the Riester pension (Riester-Rente), a widespread product with a falling number of contracts. At the end of 2025, around 14.66 million contracts still existed. Just over a fifth to just under a quarter of them are dormant, meaning no more contributions are paid into them. With the Retirement Provision Reform Act (Altersvorsorgereformgesetz) passed in spring 2026, new business ends. From 1 January 2027, the retirement investment account (Altersvorsorgedepot) takes its place. For the first time, it dispenses with the contribution guarantee. It offers a basic allowance of up to €540, €300 per child and a standard product whose reduction in yield (Effektivkosten) is capped at 1.0% a year. Existing contracts continue and can switch without losing the subsidy.

The occupational branch is salary sacrifice (Entgeltumwandlung, Section 3 no. 63 EStG, Section 1a BetrAVG, Occupational Pensions Act). In 2026, contributions of up to €8,112 a year remain tax-free, but only up to €4,056 are also exempt from social security contributions. For contributions between these limits, you save tax but no social security contributions. To the extent that the employer saves social security contributions through the conversion, it must pay in 15% of the converted pay (Section 1a(1a) BetrAVG). Collective agreements may deviate from this.

What was saved from gross pay is burdened twice in old age, with income tax and with social security contributions. Company pensions are subject to the full health insurance contribution (around 17.5% in 2026 including the average additional contribution) and the contribution to long-term care insurance (3.6%, 4.2% for people without children). The pensioner bears both contributions alone. In health insurance, only €197.75 of monthly pension remains contribution-free, while long-term care insurance only has an exemption threshold. A lump-sum payout is also subject to contributions. Under Section 229(1) sentence 3 SGB V (Social Code Book V, health insurance), it is notionally spread over 120 months and subject to contributions for ten years. In addition, salary sacrifice reduces the gross pay subject to pension insurance. This results in fewer earnings points, and sickness benefit, unemployment benefit and parental allowance turn out lower.

## Wealth from taxed income (layer 3)

The third layer includes everything built up from net income that has already been taxed, such as a securities account, a private pension or unit-linked insurance policy or a buy-to-let property. There is no state support, no age limit and no commitment. Free availability is the advantage of this layer. Capital income in the securities account is taxed on an ongoing basis at 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) plus solidarity surcharge, reduced for equity funds by a partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) of 30%. In addition, the saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag) of €1,000 or €2,000 respectively applies, as does the annual advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale), whose base interest rate (Basiszins) for 2026 is 3.20%. Rental income, by contrast, is subject to the personal tax rate.

An insurance wrapper changes the taxation, but the policy remains part of the third layer. Its returns are not taxed during the term. If a private policy is converted into an annuity, only the [[Taxable income portion (Ertragsanteil)|taxable income portion (Ertragsanteil)]] is taxable. For a pension starting at 67, that is 17% of the pension; for a pension starting at 63, it is 20%. If it is paid out as a lump sum after a term of at least twelve years and from age 62, half of the return is taxable at the personal tax rate (Section 20(1) no. 6 EStG). The two variants are mutually exclusive. How much is left at the end depends above all on the reduction in yield of the insurance wrapper.

bloecke.titel: €4,000 of gross pay after 25 years in the three layers (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: On the left is the net outlay today, on the right the result available after tax and contributions, in each case before product costs, which shift the gap in practice.

bloecke.md:
The calculation assumes a term of 25 years and a return of 5% a year. The marginal tax rate is 42% today and 28% in retirement. The 42% rate begins at a taxable income of €69,879, so the gross salary is above the contribution assessment ceiling (Beitragsbemessungsgrenze) for health and long-term care insurance of €69,750. It is assumed to stay below the pension insurance ceiling of €101,400. No product costs are included in any layer.

- In layer 1, the full €4,000 flows into the contract untaxed and grows to €13,545. Of this, 84% is taxable at 28%, so 23.5% in total. Around €10,360 remains. The net outlay today is €2,320.
- In layer 2, the conversion saves 42% tax and the 10.6% employee share of pension and unemployment insurance contributions, and therefore costs only €1,896 net. For simplicity, the tax saving is calculated on the full €4,000. Because the pension contributions saved would otherwise be deductible as pension and insurance expenses (Vorsorgeaufwendungen), it is smaller when calculated exactly. With an employer contribution of 15%, €4,600 flows in and grows to €15,577. Around 21.1% of this goes on health and long-term care insurance contributions, and the rest is taxed at 28%. Around €8,849 remains. Because the employer saves no health and long-term care contributions at this salary, it may limit its contribution to its smaller saving.
- In layer 3, €2,320 is invested after 42% tax and grows to €7,856. Of the gain of €5,536, 70% is taxable at 26.375%. Around €6,834 remains. For simplicity, the saver's allowance and the advance lump sum are not taken into account here.

The figures only compare the taxation of the layers, not products. A basic pension with a reduction in yield of 1.5% and a securities account with 0.2% would shift the result considerably. In addition, layer 1 ultimately produces a pension entitlement and not capital that you can freely dispose of.

bloecke.md:
## What each layer is suited for

The numbering says nothing about the quality of the layers. Each layer serves a different purpose.

- Layer 1 secures basic provision in old age. It pays for life, continues through every stock market phase, rules out longevity risk and is protected from seizure. For employees, it is prescribed anyway by compulsory pension insurance. For self-employed people without a professional pension scheme, it is often the only source of income that lasts until the end of their life.
- Whether layer 2 is worthwhile depends on a calculation for the individual case. It pays off when money from third parties is added, for example an employer contribution well above the statutory 15%, or allowances that result in a high subsidy rate for people on a low income with several children. Without such contributions, only a deferral effect remains, which contract costs and social security contributions on the payouts quickly cancel out.
- Layer 3 keeps the money available. Only here can money be freely withdrawn before the pension starts, inherited, reallocated or used to start a business or take a career break. In return, portfolio income and rental income are taxed on an ongoing basis. For owner-occupied residential property, however, Riester capital can also be used (Riester home ownership, Section 92a EStG).

For people on low incomes, one rule of basic income support weighs more heavily than any return assumption. In basic income support in old age, lifelong pensions from supplementary retirement provision, for example from Riester, Rürup, company or private pension contracts, are not counted up to €100 a month plus 30% of the amount above that, at most €281.50 (Section 82(4) SGB XII, Social Code Book XII). Freely available portfolio assets, by contrast, are taken into account as assets. Savers who must expect to top up their pension with basic income support in old age should therefore prefer contracts with a lifelong pension to a freely available securities account.

The layer determines when the state levies tax and how tightly the money is tied up, but not how well it is invested. There are expensive and cheap products in every layer. Choosing the layer and choosing the product are two separate decisions. Over 30 years, the choice of product usually has a greater effect on the return than the choice of layer.

A high marginal tax rate is a reason to look into layer 1, but not a sufficient reason to sign a contract. The saving arises once a year, while the commitment is for life, without surrender, lump-sum option or free inheritance. A saver who uses up the maximum amount at 45 and needs money at 52 cannot get at their contributions. An automatically lower tax rate in old age should not simply be assumed, because pensions rise, but the pension tax-free amount (Rentenfreibetrag) fixed in euros does not.

It has already been decided that the retirement investment account will replace new Riester business on 1 January 2027. For Riester home ownership, the 2% compounding of the housing subsidy account (Wohnförderkonto) is abolished for capital used for owner-occupied housing from 2028. The account is then taxed over 5 years in the payout phase instead of being spread until age 85 as before. The mothers' pension III (Mütterrente III) has also been decided. It recognises 36 instead of 30 months of child-raising periods for children born before 1992, which is around 0.5 earnings points or about €21 of monthly pension per child. For technical reasons, it will only be paid from 2028, then retrospectively.

Not yet decided is the statutory capital-funded pension based on the Swedish model with an additional contribution of 2% of gross pay, which the pension commission (Alterssicherungskommission) recommended in June 2026. For the early start pension (Frühstartrente), under which the state pays €10 a month per child from the age of six, there has been a cabinet decision since August 2026, but no law has yet been passed. Both projects are a basis for planning and not yet law in force.

mitnehmen: Layers 1 and 2 are only taxed on payout and differ in state support and payout conditions, while layer 3 is built up from taxed income; provider and asset class play no role in the classification.

The more a layer is subsidised, the more tightly the money is tied up, from layer 1 with the largest special expense deduction and the strongest commitment to layer 3 with no state support and full availability.

Deferred taxation is a deferral whose value arises from the difference in marginal tax rates between working life and retirement and from the tax-free part of the pension, and which shrinks with product costs.
For pensions starting in 2026, 84% of the pension is taxable, and because the tax-free amount is fixed as a set euro amount, every later pension increase is fully taxable.
The sensible split depends on employment status, tax rate, liquidity needs and whether basic income support might become necessary in old age, not on the number of the layer.

begriffe.text: First layer of retirement provision, comprising the statutory pension, professional pension schemes, the old-age security scheme for farmers and the Rürup pension. Only a lifelong life annuity is paid out, which cannot be terminated or capitalised, but comes with a high special expense deduction and protection from seizure.

Contributions remain tax-free or are deductible in the accumulation phase, and only the payout is taxed. This creates a deferral effect whose value depends on the difference between the marginal tax rate today and in retirement.
The year the pension starts fixes the taxable share of the pension for life. For pensions starting in 2026, it is 84%. The share rises by 0.5 percentage points per cohort and reaches 100% in 2058.

The tax-free part of the pension. It is determined in the first full year of the pension and then fixed as a set euro amount. Because it does not grow with the pension, later pension increases are fully taxable.
Taxable part of a private life annuity funded from taxed income (layer 3). It depends on the age at which the pension starts: 17% at 67, 18% at 65 or 66, 20% at 63.
